raw_case_text:
In March 2014, a 47-year-old woman was hospitalized at the Bernhard Nocht Clinic (Hamburg, Germany) with chills, nausea, and fever (temperature <40 C). The patient had a history of intravenous drug use (cocaine and benzodiazepines) and was currently enrolled in a methadone substitution program. She also had chronic hepatitis C virus infection that was successfully treated with pegylated interferon-alpha, ribavirin, and boceprevir. The patient had a sustained virologic response and negative results for hepatitis C virus RNA at follow-up without progression to liver fibrosis or cirrhosis.
At admission, her peripheral blood leukocyte count was 6.6 x 103 cells/muL, and her C-reactive protein level was increased (29 mg/L [reference value <5 mg/L]). Other routine serum and urine chemical test results were unremarkable. HIV-1/2 infection was not detected. Chest radiograph showed no abnormalities. Soft tissue abscess was not observed, but the patient admitted having injected cocaine and unknown crushed tablets intravenously the day before admission. Toxicologic screening showed highly increased levels of benzodiazepine (>5,000 ng/mL) and cocaine (>1,000 ng/mL) (reference values <20 ng/mL for both substances). Three blood cultures were collected before empiric antimicrobial therapy with intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g 1x/d) was given on day 1.
The next day, the patient's condition deteriorated. Her leukocyte count increased to 27.6 x103 cells/muL, and C-reactive protein level increased to 112 mg/L. She was highly febrile and became hypotensive and tachycardic, which are compatible with severe sepsis. The patient responded rapidly to fluid substitution, became hemodynamically stable, and did not need vasopressors. Antimicrobial therapy was changed empirically to meropenem (1,000 mg 3x/d) on day 2.
After 18 h of culture incubation, microbial growth was detected in 3 aerobic blood culture bottles inoculated at admission. Gram staining showed gram-negative rods, and matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization/time-of-flight mass spectrometry fingerprinting with direct sample deposition without extraction (Bruker Daltonim GmbH, Bremen, Germany) identified A. ursingii (score 2.19). A BLAST search (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/BLAST) of partial 16S rRNA gene sequence was performed by using a taxonomy browser (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) and showed 99% identity with the A. ursingii type strain NBRC110605 (GenBank accession no. LC014147.1).
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was performed by using Vitek 2 (bioMerieux, Nurtingen, Germany). Results showed susceptibility to imipenem (MIC <0.25 mg/mL), meropenem (<0.25 mg/mL), gentamicin (<1 mg/mL), and ciprofloxacin (<0.25 mg/mL) and resistance to ceftriaxone (32 mg/mL).
The patient became afebrile the next day, her clinical symptoms improved, and laboratory parameters of inflammation returned to reference values. Follow-up cultures remained negative. A transesophageal echocardiogram was unremarkable, without any evidence of infective endocarditis. Antimicrobial drug therapy was continued for 10 days before discharge. At follow-up 2 months later, the patient had no symptoms and was attending group-counseling sessions to maintain drug abstinence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 47-year-old woman with a history of intravenous drug use presented in March 2014 with acute fever (<40.0 °C), chills, and nausea 1 day after injecting cocaine and crushed tablets intravenously.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One day after injecting cocaine and unknown crushed tablets intravenously, the patient presented to the Bernhard Nocht Clinic in Hamburg with acute high fever, chills, and nausea. On hospital day 2, she acutely deteriorated with high fever, hypotension, tachycardia, and marked leukocytosis consistent with severe sepsis.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of intravenous drug use (cocaine and benzodiazepines), currently enrolled in a methadone maintenance program; history of chronic hepatitis C virus infection cured (sustained virologic response with negative HCV RNA and no cirrhosis) following pegylated interferon-alpha, ribavirin, and boceprevir therapy.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, and nausea; negative for local soft-tissue abscess.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: febrile (<40.0 °C) without soft-tissue abscesses. On hospital day 2: highly febrile, hypotensive, and tachycardic (responding rapidly to intravenous fluid resuscitation without vasopressors).
objective.routine_investigations: Admission WBC was 6.6 x 10^3 cells/µL and CRP was 29 mg/L (reference <5 mg/L), surging on day 2 to WBC 27.6 x 10^3 cells/µL and CRP 112 mg/L. Routine serum/urine chemistry and chest radiograph were normal; HIV-1/2 testing was negative. Urine/serum toxicology screen showed markedly elevated benzodiazepines (>5,000 ng/mL; reference <20 ng/mL) and cocaine (>1,000 ng/mL; reference <20 ng/mL).
objective.advanced_workup: Transesophageal echocardiogram (TEE) was normal without valvular vegetations or infective endocarditis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Community-acquired Acinetobacter ursingii bloodstream infection and severe sepsis following intravenous injection of cocaine and crushed tablets in an HIV-negative, HCV-cured 47-year-old female intravenous drug user. All three aerobic blood culture bottles drawn on admission flagged positive at 18 hours with Gram-negative rods identified by MALDI-TOF MS (score 2.19) and 16S rRNA gene sequencing (99% identity to A. ursingii type strain NBRC110605, GenBank LC014147.1). Vitek 2 antimicrobial susceptibility testing demonstrated resistance to ceftriaxone (MIC 32 mg/L)—explaining clinical failure on day 1 empiric IV ceftriaxone (2 g daily)—and susceptibility to imipenem (MIC <0.25 mg/L), meropenem (MIC <0.25 mg/L), gentamicin (MIC <1 mg/L), and ciprofloxacin (MIC <0.25 mg/L). Escalation on day 2 to intravenous meropenem (1,000 mg three times daily for 10 days) and IV fluid resuscitation resulted in defervescence within 24 hours, negative follow-up blood cultures, and full recovery at 2-month follow-up.
